what_its_for: Deferiprone is used to remove excess iron from your body. It is used in adults and children (3 years and older) with a condition called transfusional iron overload — this means too much iron has built up in your body because of blood transfusions. It is most commonly used in people with thalassemia and similar blood disorders.
how_to_take: Take deferiprone by mouth with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food. Swallow the tablets whole or you may split them in half if needed. If you are using the liquid (oral solution), use the measuring device that comes with your medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take it exactly as your doctor prescribes, usually 3 times a day.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight. The usual starting dose is about 25 mg per kilogram of body weight, taken 3 times a day (for a total of 75 mg/kg/day). Your doctor may adjust your dose over time depending on how well it is working and how well you tolerate it. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still close to the time you were supposed to take it. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store deferiprone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from moisture and heat. For the oral liquid solution, store it at room temperature and use it within 35 days of opening the bottle. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids or supplements that contain aluminum (such as some antacids) or other metal-containing products at the same time as deferiprone, as they may interfere with how the medicine works. Avoid drinking alcohol excessively. Tell your doctor about all vitamins and supplements you take. Do not get live vaccines without checking with your doctor first, since deferiprone can lower your white blood cell count and affect your immune system.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: fever, chills, sore throat, or other signs of infection (these may be signs of a very serious drop in white blood cells called agranulocytosis); unusual bruising or bleeding; muscle or joint pain; numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hands or feet; seizures or problems with balance and coordination; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or if you feel very unwell. You must have regular blood tests (usually weekly) to check your blood cell counts while on this medicine.
when_it_works: Deferiprone starts working to remove iron fairly quickly, but it may take several weeks to months before you notice a significant reduction in iron levels. Your doctor will monitor your iron levels with blood tests and imaging (such as MRI) over time to check how well the medicine is working. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Children (3 years and older): Deferiprone can be used in children, and the dose is based on weight. The liquid form may be easier for younger children. Pregnancy: Do not use deferiprone if you are pregnant, as it can harm the unborn baby. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking deferiprone. It is not known if it passes into breast milk, but it could harm a nursing baby. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted or this medicine may not be right for you.
